claim: Choosing where to invest in explicit engineering. The value of making an obligation explicit and its mechanizability suggest four responses, illustrated by examples. Better models and evaluation can increase mechanizability, while cheaper engineering machinery can make investment economical at lower expected benefits. Neither change implies that every obligation should be mechanized.
topology: Two columns correspond to low and high mechanizability. The low and high value rows are read top to bottom.
required_terms: From judgment-intensive to reliably mechanized (e.g., constraints, validators, or automated checks)
Higher value justifies more engineering machinery.
Example: A one-off internal naming choice.
Example: Prototype formatting— automate when it is cheap enough to maintain.
Example: Historic building design— document its fit with standards and precedent.
Example: Service dependency— block changes that violate the modeled dependency rule.
bw_encoding: Light gray marks the axes and their labels. Each white cell carries an investment choice and an example.
redesign: Separate the value of explicit engineering from how much of an obligation can be transferred to reliable machinery.
alt: Columns run from low to high mechanizability. Rows run from low to high value of making an obligation explicit. Low value suggests leaving judgment informal or mechanizing selectively. High value suggests investing in explicit judgment or in enforcement.
